claim: The subcortical sensory pathways are the fundamental channels for mapping the outside world to our minds.
source: The subcortical sensory pathways are the fundamental channels for mapping the outside world to our minds.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of subcortical sensory pathways, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Sensory pathways efficiently transmit information by adapting neural responses to the local statistics of the sensory input.
source: Sensory pathways efficiently transmit information by adapting neural responses to the local statistics of the sensory input.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about sensory pathway function.

claim: The long-standing mechanistic explanation for adaptive behaviour in sensory pathways is that neural activity decreases with increasing regularities in the local statistics of the stimuli.
source: The long-standing mechanistic explanation for this adaptive behaviour is that neural activity decreases with increasing regularities in the local statistics of the stimuli.
evidence: This describes a traditional theoretical framework in the field.

claim: An alternative account is that neural coding is directly driven by expectations of the sensory input.
source: An alternative account is that neural coding is directly driven by expectations of the sensory input.
evidence: This presents an alternative theoretical framework.

claim: Abstract expectations can drive the response amplitude to tones in the human auditory pathway.
source: The ultra-high-field functional-MRI data show that abstract expectations can drive the response amplitude to tones in the human auditory pathway.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the fMRI data presented.

claim: This study provides first unambiguous evidence of abstract processing in a subcortical sensory pathway.
source: These results provide first unambiguous evidence of abstract processing in a subcortical sensory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The neural representation of the outside world is altered by our prior beliefs even at initial points of the processing hierarchy.
source: They indicate that the neural representation of the outside world is altered by our prior beliefs even at initial points of the processing hierarchy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Expectations have measurable effects on human perception, for instance when disambiguating ambivalent stimuli like an object in the dark or spoken sentences in a noisy pub.
source: Expectations have measurable effects on human perception; for instance, when disambiguating ambivalent stimuli like an object in the dark or spoken sentences in a noisy pub (de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The predictive coding theoretical framework suggests that sensory neurons constantly match the incoming stimuli against an internal prediction derived from a generative model of the sensory input.
source: The predictive coding theoretical framework (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005) formalises the active role of expectations on perception by suggesting that sensory neurons constantly match the incoming stimuli against an internal prediction derived from a generative model of the sensory input.
evidence: This describes the predictive coding framework with supporting citations.

claim: Predictive coding increases the efficiency of encoding and naturally boosts the salience of unexpected events that often have strong relevance for behaviour and survival.
source: This strategy increases the efficiency of encoding and naturally boosts the salience of unexpected events that often have strong relevance for behaviour and survival.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of predictive coding.

claim: Predictive coding has been shown for sensory processing in the cerebral cortex.
source: Although predictive coding has been shown for sensory processing in the cerebral cortex (see Kok and de Lange, 2015 for a review), the role of predictability in subcortical sensory coding is unclear (Malmierca et al., 2019; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Parras et al., 2017; Malmierca et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The role of predictability in subcortical sensory coding is unclear.
source: Although predictive coding has been shown for sensory processing in the cerebral cortex (see Kok and de Lange, 2015 for a review), the role of predictability in subcortical sensory coding is unclear (Malmierca et al., 2019; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Parras et al., 2017; Malmierca et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations indicating ongoing debate in the field.

claim: If coding at the subcortical pathway was based on expectations on the incoming stimuli, that would mean that the brain does not hold a veridical representation of the environment even at the very early points of the processing hierarchy.
source: If coding at the subcortical pathway was based on expectations on the incoming stimuli, that would mean that the brain does not hold a veridical representation of the environment even at the very early points of the processing hierarchy.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the research question.

claim: Single neurons and neuronal ensembles of subcortical sensory pathway nuclei exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) in non-human mammals.
source: Several studies in non-human mammals (Parras et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2016; Ayala et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2014; Pérez-González et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011; Bäuerle et al., 2011; Antunes et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2009; Malmierca et al., 2009) as well as in humans (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Cacciaglia et al., 2015; Cornella et al., 2015; Escera and Malmierca, 2014; Grimm et al., 2011) have shown that single neurons and neuronal ensembles of subcortical sensory pathway nuclei exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Single neurons and neuronal ensembles of subcortical sensory pathway nuclei exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) in humans.
source: Several studies in non-human mammals (Parras et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2016; Ayala et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2014; Pérez-González et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011; Bäuerle et al., 2011; Antunes et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2009; Malmierca et al., 2009) as well as in humans (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Cacciaglia et al., 2015; Cornella et al., 2015; Escera and Malmierca, 2014; Grimm et al., 2011) have shown that single neurons and neuronal ensembles of subcortical sensory pathway nuclei exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: Neurons and neural populations showing SSA adapt to standards (frequently occurring stimuli) yet show restored responses to deviants (rarely occurring stimuli).
source: Neurons and neural populations showing SSA adapt to so-called standards (frequently occurring stimuli) yet show restored responses to so-called deviants (rarely occurring stimuli) (Ulanovsky et al., 2003; Antunes et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the SSA phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: SSA in the auditory modality is typically elicited using sequences consisting of repetitions of a standard sound incorporating a single, randomly located, deviant.
source: In the auditory modality, SSA is typically elicited using sequences consisting of repetitions of a standard sound (typically a pure tone of a given frequency) incorporating a single, randomly located, deviant (a pure tone of the same duration and loudness but with a different frequency).
evidence: This describes standard experimental methodology in the field.

claim: SSA is often taken to support the view of predictive coding.
source: Although SSA is often taken to support the view of predictive coding (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Malmierca et al., 2015; Cacciaglia et al., 2015), it can also be explained in terms of habituation (Malmierca et al., 2014), where neurons show decreased responsiveness to increased regularities in their local statistics independently of their predictability (see Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Kok and de Lange, 2015 for reviews).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies interpreting SSA as predictive coding.

claim: SSA can be explained in terms of habituation, where neurons show decreased responsiveness to increased regularities in their local statistics independently of their predictability.
source: Although SSA is often taken to support the view of predictive coding (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Malmierca et al., 2015; Cacciaglia et al., 2015), it can also be explained in terms of habituation (Malmierca et al., 2014), where neurons show decreased responsiveness to increased regularities in their local statistics independently of their predictability (see Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Kok and de Lange, 2015 for reviews).
evidence: This alternative explanation is supported by citations.

claim: Local habituation effects have been proposed to be caused by synaptic fatigue, network habituation, or sharpening of the receptive fields after stimulus repetition.
source: These local effects have been proposed to be caused by synaptic fatigue (Wang et al., 2014), network habituation (Eytan et al., 2003; Mill et al., 2011), or sharpening of the receptive fields after stimulus repetition (Grill-Spector et al., 2006); they occur even at the level of the retina (Hosoya et al., 2005) and the cochlea (Yates et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Habituation effects occur even at the level of the retina and the cochlea.
source: These local effects have been proposed to be caused by synaptic fatigue (Wang et al., 2014), network habituation (Eytan et al., 2003; Mill et al., 2011), or sharpening of the receptive fields after stimulus repetition (Grill-Spector et al., 2006); they occur even at the level of the retina (Hosoya et al., 2005) and the cochlea (Yates et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies in retina and cochlea.

claim: Habituation optimises information transmission locally by reducing responsiveness to redundant information at each stage of the processing hierarchy.
source: Habituation optimises information transmission locally by reducing responsiveness to redundant information at each stage of the processing hierarchy (Chechik et al., 2006).
evidence: This theoretical claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The predictive coding framework suggests that neural activity represents prediction error and that such prediction error is minimal for predictable stimuli independently of their local statistics.
source: In contrast, the predictive coding framework (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005) suggests that neural activity represents prediction error and that such prediction error is minimal for predictable stimuli independently of their local statistics (Malmierca et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the predictive coding framework with supporting citations.

claim: It has been previously speculated that predictive coding optimises the neural code globally; that is, that expectations formed in high-level stages of the processing hierarchy are used to adapt neural representations even at lower level stages.
source: It has been previously speculated that predictive coding optimises the neural code globally; that is, that expectations formed in high-level stages of the processing hierarchy are used to adapt neural representations even at lower level stages (Kiebel et al., 2008).
evidence: This speculative claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Distinguishing between habituation and predictive coding scenarios requires manipulating abstract predictability orthogonally to the local statistics of the stimulus.
source: Distinguishing between these two scenarios requires to manipulate abstract predictability orthogonally to the local statistics of the stimulus (Summerfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This methodological requirement is supported by a citation.

claim: The study used a novel paradigm in combination with ultra-high-field fMRI in human subjects to disassociate the habituation and predictive coding views of redundancy reduction in the auditory subcortical sensory pathway.
source: Here, we used a novel paradigm in combination with ultra-high-field fMRI in human subjects to disassociate the habituation and predictive coding views of redundancy reduction in the auditory subcortical sensory pathway.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the current study.

claim: The study focused on the nuclei of the thalamus (medial geniculate body, MGB) and midbrain (inferior colliculus, IC) as they are the key nuclei of the ascending subcortical pathway that can be reliably investigated in human participants in vivo.
source: We focused on the nuclei of the thalamus (medial geniculate body, MGB) and midbrain (inferior colliculus, IC) as they are the key nuclei of the ascending subcortical pathway that can be reliably investigated in human participants in vivo (Sitek et al., 2019).
evidence: This justifies the choice of brain regions with a citation.

claim: Blood-oxygenated-level-dependent (BOLD) responses were measured in the human subcortical auditory pathway using 7 Tesla fMRI with a spatial resolution of 1.5 mm isotropic.
source: We measured blood-oxygenated-level-dependent (BOLD) responses in the human subcortical auditory pathway using 7 Tesla fMRI with a spatial resolution of 1.5 mm isotropic.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: A slab comprising the MGB and the IC was recorded.
source: We recorded a slab comprising the MGB and the IC.
evidence: This describes the imaging acquisition.

claim: Nineteen subjects listened to sequences of eight pure tones (seven repetitions of a standard and one deviant tone).
source: Nineteen subjects listened to sequences of eight pure tones (seven repetitions of a standard and one deviant tone; see Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with reference to a figure.

claim: Tones were taken from a pool of three tones and used equally often as standards and as deviants.
source: Tones were taken from a pool of three tones and used equally often as standards and as deviants.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design.

claim: Subjects reported the position of the deviant for each sequence by pressing one button of a response box as quickly as possible.
source: Subjects reported the position of the deviant for each sequence by pressing one button of a response box as quickly as possible.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task.

claim: All subjects showed ceiling performances to all deviant positions (90 ± 3%, 95 ± 1%, and 94 ± 2%; mean accuracies ± standard error of the mean, for deviants in positions 4, 5 and 6, respectively).
source: All subjects showed ceiling performances to all deviant positions (90 ± 3%, 95 ± 1%, and 94 ± 2%; mean accuracies ± standard error of the mean, for deviants in positions 4, 5 and 6, respectively), indicating that subjects were attentive.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data.

claim: Ceiling performance indicates that subjects were attentive.
source: All subjects showed ceiling performances to all deviant positions (90 ± 3%, 95 ± 1%, and 94 ± 2%; mean accuracies ± standard error of the mean, for deviants in positions 4, 5 and 6, respectively), indicating that subjects were attentive.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: The response profile showed that the more expected the deviants, the more reduced the responses, fitting with the predictive coding hypothesis.
source: On visual inspection, the response profile showed that the more expected the deviants, the more reduced the responses, fitting with h2 (the predictive coding hypothesis; Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the data with reference to a figure.

claim: MGB and IC mesoscopic responses to deviant tones cannot be explained by habituation only.
source: The results of these tests show that MGB and IC mesoscopic responses to deviant tones cannot be explained by habituation only.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical tests.

claim: Deviance detection can be virtually abolished at the mesoscopic level by manipulating subjects' expectations; that is, by rendering the deviant predictable.
source: Thus, deviance detection can be virtually abolished at the mesoscopic level by manipulating subjects' expectations; that is, by rendering the deviant predictable.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Posterior probability maps showed that most voxels in both ICs and MGBs were more likely to respond according to the principles of predictive coding.
source: Posterior maps showed that most voxels in both ICs and MGBs were more likely to respond according to the principles of predictive coding (red sections in Figure 4B).
evidence: This reports Bayesian model comparison results with reference to a figure.

claim: For the IC, 98% (right IC) and 86% (left IC) of the voxels were more likely driven by predictive coding.
source: For the IC, this was the case for 98% (right IC) and 86% (left IC) of the voxels.
evidence: This reports the proportion of voxels best explained by predictive coding.

claim: Only negligible parts of the four nuclei (maximum of 3%) were more likely to be driven by habituation.
source: Only negligible parts of the four nuclei (maximum of 3%) were more likely to be driven by habituation (blue sections in Figure 4B).
evidence: This reports the proportion of voxels best explained by habituation with reference to a figure.

claim: The ventral MGB (vMGB) is the primary or lemniscal subsection of the MGB.
source: The ventral tonotopic gradient was identified as the ventral MGB (vMGB) which is the primary or lemniscal subsection of the MGB (see Figure 5A, green).
evidence: This is based on a previous study with reference to a figure.

claim: Similar distributions of the SSA index were observed in the vMGB and the rest of the MGB.
source: Similar distributions of the SI were observed in the vMGB and the rest of the MGB (Figure 5B).
evidence: This reports comparison of SSA indices with reference to a figure.

claim: Similar distributions of the posterior probability of the habituation and predictive coding model were observed across the voxels of each of the subdivisions of the MGB.
source: We also observed similar distributions of the posterior probability of the habituation and predictive coding model across the voxels of each of the subdivisions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This reports Bayesian model comparison results with reference to a figure.

claim: Predictive coding was the most likely underlying model in the entire left and right vMGB, respectively, and in 97% and 93% of the left and right voxels not belonging to the ventral subdivision.
source: Predictive coding was the most likely underlying model in the entire left and right vMGB, respectively, and in 97% and 93% of the left and right voxels not belonging to the ventral subdivision.
evidence: This reports the proportion of voxels best explained by predictive coding in MGB subdivisions.

claim: Both the vMGB and the rest of the MGB are dominated by responses driven by predictive coding.
source: We conclude that both the vMGB and the rest of the MGB are dominated by responses driven by predictive coding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Bayesian model comparison.

claim: BOLD responses in most voxels (a minimum of 96%) of the four nuclei are best explained by the level of predictability of both the deviants and standards.
source: BOLD responses in most voxels (a minum of 96%) of the four nuclei are best explained by the level of predictability of both the deviants and standards (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This reports Bayesian model comparison results with reference to figures.

claim: Mean BOLD responses in IC and MGB correlated with the subjects' expectations of the probability of the stimulus occurrence but not with the local stimulus statistics.
source: First, mean BOLD responses in IC and MGB correlated with the subjects' expectations of the probability of the stimulus occurrence but not with the local stimulus statistics.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings.

claim: Events deviating from local stimulus statistics did not lead to increased responses in IC and MGB if subjects expected these events.
source: Second, events deviating from local stimulus statistics did not lead to increased responses in IC and MGB if subjects expected these events.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings.

claim: Bayesian model comparison showed that the responses of the majority of voxels in IC and MGB are best explained by a predictive coding model.
source: Third, Bayesian model comparison showed that the responses of the majority of voxels in IC and MGB are best explained by a predictive coding model.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings.

claim: The findings indicate that sensory processing in auditory midbrain and thalamus are mostly driven by expectations of the subject and not by regularities in the local stimulus statistics.
source: Together, the findings indicate that sensory processing in auditory midbrain and thalamus are mostly driven by expectations of the subject and not by regularities in the local stimulus statistics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Several previous studies have interpreted response properties of subcortical sensory nuclei within a predictive coding framework.
source: Several previous studies have interpreted response properties of subcortical sensory nuclei within a predictive coding framework (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Parras et al., 2017; Malmierca et al., 2015; Cacciaglia et al., 2015; Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous studies on subcortical predictive coding have used designs where predictions were generated based on the regularities of the local stimulus statistics.
source: These studies have, however, used designs where predictions were generated based on the regularities of the local stimulus statistics.
evidence: This is a critique of previous studies based on methodological analysis.

claim: Mesoscopic responses to violation of abstract rules have been reported in the sensory cortex.
source: Although mesoscopic responses to violation of abstract rules have been reported in the sensory cortex (e.g., Näätänen et al., 1978; Paavilainen, 2013; Kok and de Lange, 2015; de Lange et al., 2018), they have not been reported in subcortical nuclei to-date.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to cortical studies.

claim: Mesoscopic responses to violation of abstract rules have not been reported in subcortical nuclei to-date.
source: Although mesoscopic responses to violation of abstract rules have been reported in the sensory cortex (e.g., Näätänen et al., 1978; Paavilainen, 2013; Kok and de Lange, 2015; de Lange et al., 2018), they have not been reported in subcortical nuclei to-date.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The current study breaks with a long tradition on research on subcortical SSA by defining the predictions based on abstract rules that were orthogonal to the regularity of the stimulus local statistics.
source: Our study breaks with a long tradition on research on subcortical SSA (Font-Alaminos et al., 2020; Parras et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2016; Cacciaglia et al., 2015; Duque and Malmierca, 2015; Ayala et al., 2015; Cornella et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2014; Anderson and Malmierca, 2013; Ayala et al., 2012; Pérez-González et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011; Bäuerle et al., 2011; Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; Antunes et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2009; Malmierca et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2009) by defining the predictions based on abstract rules that were orthogonal to the regularity of the stimulus local statistics.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the current study with extensive citations to previous work.

claim: Only one study attempted to investigate the impact of abstract rules on SSA using alternating tone sequences in anaesthetised rats.
source: Only one study attempted to investigate the impact of abstract rules on SSA using alternating tone sequences in anaesthetised rats (Malmierca et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: A study on SSA in the rodent auditory system reported that structures at increasingly higher stages of the auditory pathway show increasing amounts of prediction error.
source: A study on SSA in the rodent auditory system (Parras et al., 2017) where predictability was controlled using local stimulus statistics reported that structures at increasingly higher stages of the auditory pathway show increasing amounts of prediction error.
evidence: This reports findings from a cited study.

claim: Parras et al. 2017 defined prediction error as the responses to sounds that deviate from the predictions in comparison to the responses to those same sounds when there were no available predictions.
source: The authors defined prediction error as the responses to sounds that deviate from the predictions in comparison to the responses to those same sounds when there were no available predictions.
evidence: This describes the methodology of a cited study.

claim: Parras et al. 2017 concluded that the IC, MGB, and AC form a hierarchical network of prediction error.
source: The authors concluded that the IC, MGB, and AC form a hierarchical network of prediction error.
evidence: This reports the conclusion of a cited study.

claim: The current study's findings contrast with Parras' results, where the IC showed little or no difference between the responses elicited by deviant and control sounds.
source: This contrast with Parras' results, where the IC showed little or no difference between the responses elicited by deviant and control sounds.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and a previous study.

claim: Nuclei in the auditory pathway are organised in primary (or lemniscal) and secondary (or non-lemniscal) subdivisions.
source: Nuclei in the auditory pathway are organised in primary (or lemniscal) and secondary (or non-lemniscal) subdivisions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory pathway organization.

claim: The lemniscal division of the auditory pathway has narrowly tuned frequency responses and is considered as responsible for the transmission of bottom-up information.
source: The lemniscal division of the auditory pathway has narrowly tuned frequency responses and is considered as responsible for the transmission of bottom-up information; the non-lemniscal division presents wider tuned frequency responses and is also involved in multisensory integration (Hu, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The non-lemniscal division presents wider tuned frequency responses and is also involved in multisensory integration.
source: The lemniscal division of the auditory pathway has narrowly tuned frequency responses and is considered as responsible for the transmission of bottom-up information; the non-lemniscal division presents wider tuned frequency responses and is also involved in multisensory integration (Hu, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: In the animal neurophysiology literature the strongest SSA is typically reported in non-lemniscal areas; that is, in dorsal and medial sections of the MGB and the cortices of the IC.
source: In the animal neurophysiology literature the strongest SSA is typically reported in non-lemniscal areas; that is, in dorsal and medial sections of the MGB (Antunes et al., 2010; Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; Duque et al., 2014) and the cortices of the IC (Pérez-González et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2014; Duque et al., 2014; Ayala and Malmierca, 2015; Ayala and Malmierca, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Subdivisions of IC and MGB are notoriously difficult to assess in humans in vivo because of their small size and deep location within the brain.
source: Subdivisions of IC and MGB are notoriously difficult to assess in humans in vivo because of their small size and deep location within the brain (Moerel et al., 2015; Mihai et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The predictive coding model is the most likely generator of the data across the entire IC nuclei.
source: Nevertheless, our results show that the predictive coding model is the most likely generator of the data across the entire nuclei.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Bayesian model comparison.

claim: Predictive coding underlies encoding of both lemniscal and non-lemniscal subdivisions of the IC and MGB.
source: We therefore assume that predictive coding underlies encoding of both, lemniscal and non-lemniscal subdivisions of the IC and MGB.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis.

claim: The fundamental difference with the animal literature might stem from the design involving an active task: lemniscal pathways might only be strongly modulated by predictions when they carry behaviourally relevant sensory information.
source: First, our design involved an active task: lemniscal pathways might only be strongly modulated by predictions when they carry behaviourally relevant sensory information.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences with animal studies.

claim: The modulation of the subcortical pathways might be fundamentally different in humans compared to other mammals.
source: Second, the modulation of the subcortical pathways might be fundamentally different in humans compared to other mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences with animal studies.

claim: Given the strength of the SSA effects reported in this study, it is possible that regions with weak SSA might have been contaminated with signal stemming from areas with strong SSA due to smoothing and interpolation necessary for the analysis of fMRI data.
source: Last, given the strength of the SSA effects reported in this study, it is possible that regions with weak SSA might have been contaminated with signal stemming from areas with strong SSA due to smoothing and interpolation necessary for the analysis of fMRI data.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings considering methodological limitations.

claim: It is tempting to hypothesise that the predictions on the sensory input that drive the subcortical responses in our experiment are generated in the cerebral cortex.
source: It is tempting to hypothesise that the predictions on the sensory input that drive the subcortical responses in our experiment are generated in the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis.

claim: The hypothesis that predictions are generated in the cerebral cortex would be consistent with the strong feedback connections from cerebral cortex to the subcortical sensory pathway.
source: This hypothesis would be consistent with the strong feedback connections from cerebral cortex to the subcortical sensory pathway (Winer, 1984; Winer, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations about anatomical connectivity.

claim: The hypothesis that predictions are generated in the cerebral cortex would be consistent with the results from animal studies where the deactivation of unilateral auditory cortex or the TRN led to reduction of SSA in the ventral MGB.
source: It would also be consistent with the results from animal studies where the deactivation of unilateral auditory cortex (Bäuerle et al., 2011) or the TRN (Yu et al., 2009) led to reduction of SSA in the ventral MGB (but also see contradictory findings in non-lemniscal MGB, Antunes and Malmierca, 2011, and non-lemniscal IC, Anderson and Malmierca, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: The paradigm was optimised to study prediction error rather than the generation of such predictions.
source: Our paradigm was optimised to study prediction error rather than the generation of such predictions, and we lacked the resolution to study cortical responses in enough detail as to disentangle activity representing predictions from activity representing prediction error.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The study lacked the resolution to study cortical responses in enough detail as to disentangle activity representing predictions from activity representing prediction error.
source: Our paradigm was optimised to study prediction error rather than the generation of such predictions, and we lacked the resolution to study cortical responses in enough detail as to disentangle activity representing predictions from activity representing prediction error.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Although it is unlikely that subcortical sensory nuclei like the MGB or IC are able to generate predictions based on the task instructions, whether these predictions originate in the cerebral cortex remains an open question.
source: Thus, although it is unlikely that subcortical sensory nuclei like the MGB or IC are able to generate predictions based on the task instructions, whether these predictions originate in the cerebral cortex remains an open question.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the source of predictions.

claim: Higher BOLD responses to attended in contrast to unattended sounds are present in auditory cortex.
source: Higher BOLD responses to attended in contrast to unattended sounds are present in auditory cortex (Lee et al., 2014; Paltoglou et al., 2011), and to a much weaker extend also in the IC (Rinne et al., 2007; Rinne et al., 2008; Varghese et al., 2015; Riecke et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Higher BOLD responses to attended in contrast to unattended sounds are present to a much weaker extent in the IC.
source: Higher BOLD responses to attended in contrast to unattended sounds are present in auditory cortex (Lee et al., 2014; Paltoglou et al., 2011), and to a much weaker extend also in the IC (Rinne et al., 2007; Rinne et al., 2008; Varghese et al., 2015; Riecke et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The strong attenuation of responses to fully expected deviants at position 6 might not only be interpreted in terms of predictive coding, but also additionally by attentional gain modulation.
source: This strong attenuation might not only be interpreted in terms of predictive coding, but also additionally by attentional gain modulation: deviants with a posterior probability of 1 might not need to be examined as carefully as deviants with low posterior probability, because its occurrence is guaranteed by task design.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Deviance detection is salient even in anaesthetised animals.
source: From previous work in animals, we know that deviance detection is salient even in anaesthetised animals (Malmierca et al., 2015) and effect sizes of SSA in the IC are comparable in the awake and anaesthetised mouse (Duque and Malmierca, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Effect sizes of SSA in the IC are comparable in the awake and anaesthetised mouse.
source: From previous work in animals, we know that deviance detection is salient even in anaesthetised animals (Malmierca et al., 2015) and effect sizes of SSA in the IC are comparable in the awake and anaesthetised mouse (Duque and Malmierca, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Cacciaglia et al. 2015 showed deviance detection in the human subcortical auditory pathway in passive listening conditions.
source: Using fMRI in humans, Cacciaglia and colleagues (Cacciaglia et al., 2015) showed deviance detection in the human subcortical auditory pathway in passive listening conditions.
evidence: This reports findings from a cited study.

claim: Stimulus-specific adaptation at early stages of the sensory pathways has been reported in the visual, olfactory, and somatosensory pathways.
source: Stimulus-specific adaptation at early stages of the sensory pathways has, however, also been reported in the visual (Dhruv and Carandini, 2014), olfactory (Fletcher and Wilson, 2003), and somatosensory (Maravall et al., 2013) pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies in other sensory modalities.

claim: Predictive coding serves to optimise the dynamic range of sensory systems.
source: Predictive coding serves to optimise the dynamic range of sensory systems (Brenner et al., 2000), and to maximise information transmission in the neural code by reducing the responses to expected stimuli (Fairhall et al., 2001) and to redundant portions of the incoming sensory signal (Huang and Rao, 2011).
evidence: This theoretical claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Predictive coding serves to maximise information transmission in the neural code by reducing the responses to expected stimuli and to redundant portions of the incoming sensory signal.
source: Predictive coding serves to optimise the dynamic range of sensory systems (Brenner et al., 2000), and to maximise information transmission in the neural code by reducing the responses to expected stimuli (Fairhall et al., 2001) and to redundant portions of the incoming sensory signal (Huang and Rao, 2011).
evidence: This theoretical claim is supported by citations.

claim: Abstract expectations are likely used in other sensory modalities to facilitate sensory processing in subcortical sensory nuclei.
source: We speculate that abstract expectations are used as well in other sensory modalities to facilitate sensory processing in subcortical sensory nuclei.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Atypical predictive coding in the subcortical sensory pathway is expected to result in profound repercussion at the cognitive level.
source: Given the importance of predictive coding on sensory processing (e.g., Sohoglu and Davis, 2016; Davis and Johnsrude, 2007), atypical predictive coding in the subcortical sensory pathway is expected to result in profound repercussion at the cognitive level (McFadyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations.

claim: Individuals with developmental dyslexia have altered adaption dynamics to stimulus regularities.
source: For instance, individuals with developmental dyslexia, a disorder that is characterised by difficulties with processing speech sounds, have altered adaption dynamics to stimulus regularities (Perrachione et al., 2016; Ahissar et al., 2006; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), altered responses in the left MGB (Díaz et al., 2012; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), and atypical left hemispheric cortico-thalamic pathways (Müller-Axt et al., 2017; Tschentscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to dyslexia studies.

claim: Individuals with developmental dyslexia have altered responses in the left MGB.
source: For instance, individuals with developmental dyslexia, a disorder that is characterised by difficulties with processing speech sounds, have altered adaption dynamics to stimulus regularities (Perrachione et al., 2016; Ahissar et al., 2006; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), altered responses in the left MGB (Díaz et al., 2012; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), and atypical left hemispheric cortico-thalamic pathways (Müller-Axt et al., 2017; Tschentscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to dyslexia studies.

claim: Individuals with developmental dyslexia have atypical left hemispheric cortico-thalamic pathways.
source: For instance, individuals with developmental dyslexia, a disorder that is characterised by difficulties with processing speech sounds, have altered adaption dynamics to stimulus regularities (Perrachione et al., 2016; Ahissar et al., 2006; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), altered responses in the left MGB (Díaz et al., 2012; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009), and atypical left hemispheric cortico-thalamic pathways (Müller-Axt et al., 2017; Tschentscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to dyslexia studies.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms underlying SSA and its relation to sensory processing in subcortical sensory pathways could have valuable applications in clinical contexts.
source: Understanding the mechanisms underlying SSA and its relation to sensory processing in subcortical sensory pathways could have valuable applications in clinical contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics committee of the Medical Faculty of the University of Leipzig, Germany (ethics approval number 273/14-ff).
source: This study was approved by the Ethics committee of the Medical Faculty of the University of Leipzig, Germany (ethics approval number 273/14-ff).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All listeners provided written informed consent and received monetary compensation for their participation.
source: All listeners provided written informed consent and received monetary compensation for their participation.
evidence: This describes the consent process.

claim: Nineteen German native speakers (12 female), aged 24 to 34 years (mean 26.6), participated in the study.
source: Nineteen German native speakers (12 female), aged 24 to 34 years (mean 26.6), participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: None of the participants reported a history of psychiatric or neurological disorders, hearing difficulties, or current use of psychoactive medications.
source: None of them reported a history of psychiatric or neurological disorders, hearing difficulties, or current use of psychoactive medications.
evidence: This describes participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Normal hearing abilities were confirmed with pure tone audiometry (250 Hz to 8000 Hz) with a threshold equal to or below 25 dB SPL.
source: Normal hearing abilities were confirmed with pure tone audiometry (250 Hz to 8000 Hz; Madsen Micromate 304, GN Otometrics, Denmark) with a threshold equal to or below 25 dB SPL.
evidence: This describes the hearing screening procedure.

claim: All sounds were 50 ms long (including 5 ms in/out ramps) pure tones of frequencies 1455 Hz, 1500 Hz, or 1600 Hz.
source: All sounds were 50 ms long (including 5 ms in/out ramps) pure tones of frequencies 1455 Hz, 1500 Hz, or 1600 Hz, corresponding to three local minima of the power spectrum of the noise produced by the MRI during the scanning.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: The tone frequencies corresponded to three local minima of the power spectrum of the noise produced by the MRI during the scanning.
source: All sounds were 50 ms long (including 5 ms in/out ramps) pure tones of frequencies 1455 Hz, 1500 Hz, or 1600 Hz, corresponding to three local minima of the power spectrum of the noise produced by the MRI during the scanning.
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing specific frequencies.

claim: Six standard-deviant frequency combinations were constructed from the three tones and used the same number of times across each run.
source: From those three tones, we constructed six standard-deviant frequency combinations that were used the same number of times across each run, so that all tones were used the same number of times as deviant and standards.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Three rather than two tones were used so that each run contained six rather than two different standard-deviant combinations, rendering the task more engaging.
source: We used three rather than two tones so that each run contained six rather than two different standard-deviant combinations, rendering the task more engaging.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the design choice.

claim: Stimuli were separated by 700 ms inter-stimulus-intervals (ISI), amounting to a total duration of 5300 ms per sequence.
source: Stimuli were separated by 700 ms inter-stimulus-intervals (ISI), amounting to a total duration of 5300 ms per sequence.
evidence: This describes the timing parameters.

claim: A pilot behavioural study was run to choose the ISI, measuring the reaction time to deviants 4, 5, and 6 with different ISIs.
source: To choose the ISI, we run a pilot behavioural study where we measured the reaction time to deviants 4, 5, and 6 with different ISIs.
evidence: This describes the pilot study conducted.

claim: The shortest possible ISI that allowed the subjects to predict the fully expected deviant was chosen, as revealed by a significant behavioural benefit in the RT for a deviant located in position 6.
source: We took the shortest possible ISI that allowed the subjects to predict the fully expected deviant, as revealed by a significant behavioural benefit in the RT for a deviant located in position 6.
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing the ISI.

claim: The inter-trial-interval (ITI) was jittered so that deviants were separated by an average of 5 s, up to a maximum of 11 s, with a minimum ITI of 1500 ms.
source: The inter-trial-interval (ITI) was jittered so that deviants were separated by an average of 5 s, up to a maximum of 11 s, with a minimum ITI of 1500 ms.
evidence: This describes the timing design.

claim: The ITI properties were chosen to maximise the efficiency of the response estimation of the deviants, while keeping a sufficiently long ITI to ensure that the sequences belonging to separate trials were not confounded.
source: We chose such ITI properties to maximise the efficiency of the response estimation of the deviants (Friston et al., 1999), while keeping a sufficiently long ITI to ensure that the sequences belonging to separate trials were not confounded.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the ITI design with a citation.

claim: The experiment consisted in four runs with the same task.
source: The experiment consisted in four runs with the same task.
evidence: This describes the experimental structure.

claim: Each run contained 6 blocks of 10 trials.
source: Each run contained 6 blocks of 10 trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental structure.

claim: The 10 trials in each block used one of the six possible combinations of pure tones, so that all the sequences within each block had the same standard and deviant.
source: The 10 trials in each block used one of the six possible combinations of pure tones, so that all the sequences within each block had the same standard and deviant.
evidence: This describes the block design.

claim: Within a block only the position of the deviant was unknown, while the frequency of the deviant was known.
source: Thus, within a block only the position of the deviant was unknown, while the frequency of the deviant was known.
evidence: This describes what information was available to participants.

claim: The order of the blocks within the experiment was randomised.
source: The order of the blocks within the experiment was randomised.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure.

claim: The position of the deviant was pseudorandomised across all trials in each run so that each deviant position happened exactly 20 times per run but an unknown amount of times per block.
source: The position of the deviant was pseudorandomised across all trials in each run so that each deviant position happened exactly 20 times per run but an unknown amount of times per block.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure.

claim: This constraint allowed keeping the same a priori probability for all deviant positions in each block.
source: This constraint allowed us to keep the same a priori probability for all deviant positions in each block.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the randomization procedure.

claim: There were 23 silent gaps of 5300 ms duration (i.e., null events of the same duration as the tone sequences) randomly located in each run.
source: In addition, there were 23 silent gaps of 5300 ms duration (i.e., null events of the same duration as the tone sequences) randomly located in each run (Friston et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the inclusion of null events with a citation.

claim: Each run lasted around 10 minutes, depending on the reaction times of the participant.
source: Each run lasted around 10 minutes, depending on the reaction times of the participant.
evidence: This describes the duration of the runs.

claim: The runs were separated by breaks of a minimum of 1 minute, during which the subjects could rest.
source: The runs were separated by breaks of a minimum of 1 minute, during which the subjects could rest.
evidence: This describes the break periods.

claim: Fieldmaps and a whole-head EPI were acquired between the second and third run.
source: Fieldmaps and a whole-head EPI (see Data acquisition) were acquired between the second and third run.
evidence: This describes the acquisition timing.

claim: The first run was preceded by a practice run of four randomly chosen trials to ensure the subjects had understood the task.
source: The first run was preceded by a practice run of four randomly chosen trials to ensure the subjects had understood the task.
evidence: This describes the practice procedure.

claim: fMRI was acquired during the practice run in order to allow the subjects to undertake the training with MRI-noise.
source: We acquired fMRI during the practice run in order to allow the subjects to undertake the training with MRI-noise.
evidence: This explains the rationale for acquiring fMRI during practice.

claim: MRI data were acquired using a Siemens Magnetom 7 Tesla scanner with an eight-channel head coil.
source: MRI data were acquired using a Siemens Magnetom 7 Tesla scanner (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) with an eight-channel head coil (RAPID Biomedical, Rimpar, Germany).
evidence: This describes the MRI equipment.

claim: Functional MRI data were acquired using echo planar imaging (EPI) sequences with a field of view (FoV) of 132 mm × 132 mm and partial coverage with 30 slices.
source: Functional MRI data were acquired using echo planar imaging (EPI) sequences. We used a field of view (FoV) of 132 mm × 132 mm and partial coverage with 30 slices.
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: The fMRI volume was oriented in parallel to the superior temporal gyrus such that the slices encompassed the IC, the MGB, and the superior temporal gyrus.
source: This volume was oriented in parallel to the superior temporal gyrus such that the slices encompassed the IC, the MGB, and the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: This describes the slice positioning.

claim: Three volumes of an additional whole-head EPI with the same parameters and 80 slices were acquired during resting to aid the coregistration process.
source: In addition, we acquired three volumes of an additional whole-head EPI with the same parameters (including the FoV) and 80 slices during resting to aid the coregistration process (see Data preprocessing).
evidence: This describes additional data acquisition for coregistration.

claim: During fMRI data acquisition, heart rate and respiration rate were acquired using a BIOPAC MP150 system.
source: During fMRI data acquisition, heart rate and respiration rate were acquired using a BIOPAC MP150 system (BIOPAC Systems Inc, Goleta, CA, USA).
evidence: This describes the physiological monitoring.

claim: Structural images were recorded using an MP2RAGE T1 protocol with 700 µm isotropic resolution.
source: Structural images were recorded using an MP2RAGE (Marques et al., 2010) T1 protocol with 700 µm isotropic resolution, TE = 2.45 ms, TR = 5000 ms, TI1 = 900 ms, TI2 = 2750 ms, flip angle 1 = 5°, flip angle 2 = 3°, FoV = 224 mm × 224 mm, GRAPPA acceleration factor 2.
evidence: This describes the structural imaging parameters with a citation.

claim: Stimuli were presented using MATLAB with the Psychophysics Toolbox extensions and delivered through an MrConfon amplifier and headphones.
source: Stimuli were presented using MATLAB (The Mathworks Inc, Natick, MA, USA; RRID:SCR_001622) with the Psychophysics Toolbox extensions (Brainard, 1997) and delivered through an MrConfon amplifier and headphones (MrConfon GmbH, Magdeburg, Germany).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation system with citations.

claim: Loudness was adjusted independently for each subject before starting the data acquisition to a comfortable level.
source: Loudness was adjusted independently for each subject before starting the data acquisition to a comfortable level.
evidence: This describes the loudness calibration procedure.
